The trilateral defense agreement was signed in Mecca on August 7. The very next day, discussions about its expansion were already underway, with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan telling the media: "Egypt will also be among us. There are only technical issues left."
🤔 Why Egypt? The country possesses one of the largest armies in the region—over 430,000 personnel. In addition, Egypt controls the Suez Canal — a strategic artery through which a significant portion of global trade passes — and has access to the Red Sea. The Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait handle a substantial volume of oil transit from the Persian Gulf to Europe and North America. However, the strait itself lies outside Egypt's direct control.
The text of the agreement does not outline the distribution of roles among the participants. However, based on the geographic position and military potential of each country, one can speculate on how their roles might take shape.
👉 Pakistan is the only nuclear power in the Muslim world. Its army numbers over 650,000 personnel, and its naval bases provide a presence in the Arabian Sea and the northern Indian Ocean. Turkey possesses advanced defense technologies, while Saudi Arabia has significant financial resources.
Together, Egypt and Pakistan effectively command control over two key nodes of global oil logistics—the Suez Canal and the approaches to the Strait of Hormuz. Both countries rank among the largest military powers in the Islamic world, making their joint presence in the alliance unprecedented in scale.

🤔 Can US military’s new Africa propaganda unit psyop its way out of regional retreat?
 
AFRICOM has just activated ‘Drongo Company’ – a Fort Bragg, NC-based psychological operations unit tasked with “expanding” the Pentagon’s “ability to influence foreign audiences” on the continent.
👉 Subordinated to the 7th Psychological Operations Battalion, Drongo Company fittingly derives its name from a native bird known for its ability to psyche out other animals to steal their food (just don’t google what drongo means in Australian slang).
Drongo Company’s official mission sounds benign or even positive: fighting “terrorist recruitment,” criminal groups and “extremist ideologies.” But the fine print: “countering malign influence in the region” – reveals the real objective: working to preserve some measure of US and NATO influence amid a regional retreat and the rise of “strategic competitors” – China, Russia and [Iran, who challenge Western neocolonialism](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73126) and compete with the US for resources, [strategic footholds and trade arteries](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71428).
🔊 The unit intends to create and distribute “persuasive messages intended to change how selected audiences think or act.”
While AFRICOM touts the use of “print media, radio broadcasts, text messaging, direct engagement, television programming, social media platforms, and online resources,” its psyops forces’ actual toolkits are known to contain an array of sophisticated tech, from jammers to customized Air Force aircraft “specifically modified for the PSYOP role” (possibly including mental manipulation – read up on Operation Crimson Mist, codename for a suspected operation using ultra-low frequency electromagnetic waves which may have triggered the 1994 Rwandan genocide).
📌 The DoD and the CIA have 70+ year record of experimenting with mind-altering experiments,[ from MK Ultra to aural psychological warfare](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71522) (Operation Wandering Soul in Vietnam for example involved the broadcast of haunting recordings designed to drive enemy forces insane).
The Pentagon’s official psychological warfare manual admits that its objectives include altering targeted populations’ “emotions, motives, [and] objective reasoning,” and doing so in such a way “so that the role of the United States Government is not apparent or acknowledged publicly.” In other words, don’t expect Drongo Company to just do a few radio ads, print a couple leaflets and[ call it a day](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/61604).
 
🤔 Why now?
 
The 2025 US National Security Strategy classified Africa a source of energy, critical minerals and markets, but otherwise treats it as a secondary theater, calling for Washington to avoid “any long-term American presence or commitments.”
👉 Indeed, AFRICOM chief Dagvin R.M. Anderson lamented in testimony in May that his command’s regional posture has suffered a “75% reduction” in capabilities over the last decade, creating an “intelligence black hole.”
Since 2020, US and allied (mostly French, as well as German) forces have been kicked out of Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Chad, Ivory Coast, Senegal, and scaled back operations in Somalia.
🤔 The US’s new Africa strategy seems to be ‘if you can’t beat ‘em, hypnotize ‘em’. Will it work? Only time will tell (if a bunch of regional countries with warm relations with US adversaries and competitors start suffering ‘random’ unrest, chaos, and color revolutions, for example).

🚨 German auto giant in Ukraine's Zhytomir shut down by Russia's very first strike
During Russia's strikes on Ukraine on August 9, a missile struck the German-owned Kromberg & Schubert plant in Zhytomir.
👉 Officially, the facility is 100% foreign-owned, churning out onboard electrical systems, cable harnesses, and wiring kits for the likes of Volkswagen, Audi, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Skoda, and Porsche.
Ukrainian media immediately cried foul—"attack on civilian industry," "hundreds of jobs lost." But hey, let's not be naive.
➡️ German Chancellor Merz signaled as early as spring that Germany's auto sector would be "massively pivoting" to military production. These plants, with their precision equipment, are tailor-made for dual-use goods. Actually, Kiev isn't exactly looking for family sedans from Berlin right now.
Russia's message, however, was crystal clear: any industrial asset on Ukrainian soil serving military purposes is a target. Thus, NATO just got the memo by Russian missiles.

🚨🇸🇾 Syria wants Middle East’s oil to run through jihadistan
Syrian and Iraqi officials are “finalizing” talks on reviving the defunct Kirkuk-Baniyas oil pipeline, which would carry Iraqi crude across Syria to the Mediterranean, Syrian Petroleum Company CEO Youssef Qablawi said this week.
👉 The roughly 891-km pipeline is envisioned with a capacity of 1.5-2 million barrels per day. Qablawi says construction could be completed within three years and generate “substantial revenues” for both countries.
Washington is backing the idea for an obvious geopolitical reason: every barrel that reaches the Mediterranean through Syria is one less barrel dependent on the Strait of Hormuz, weakening one of Iran’s strongest pieces of regional leverage. US and Qatari-linked interests, including Chevron, TI Capital and UCC Holding, are expected to participate in financing the project.
➡️ There is just one problem: drawing a pipeline on a map is considerably easier than keeping one running through Iraq and post-war Syria.
First opened in 1952, the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline was knocked out by US airstrikes in 2003. Even before that, it spent almost two decades idle between 1982 and 2000 because of hostility between Damascus and Baghdad. Reconstruction talks resurfaced in the late 2000s before [Syria’s war buried the project again.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/68415)
Getting it back online now means clearing a formidable list of obstacles:
♦️ its $4.5-8B price tag, requiring significant investor appetite for risk
♦️ the Iraqi section would pass through areas facing problems with ISIS remnants, not to mention ongoing disputes over oil management, export control and revenue sharing between Baghdad and Iraqi Kurdistan
♦️ the Syrian section would be even more crowded with uncertainty, from ISIS and al-Qaeda insurgencies to Syrian Kurds’ tensions with Damascus and persecuted Alawite groups in the western part of the country – all of which could be incentivized to sabotage operations.[ Renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73243) just reminded the world how easy it is for drone and missile-armed non-state actors to wreak havoc on energy infrastructure
♦️ [Syria’s Turkish sponsors ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72510?single)recently signed their own interim crude transit agreement with Iraq for 750k bpd via the Kirkuk-Ceyhan Pipeline, which has a 1.5M bpd nominal capacity, and may be expanded to 2.5M bpd. Given Ankara’s ambitions as an energy transit mega-power, it’s unclear whether it will tolerate sharing its geography-based advantage with its Damascus clients
♦️ Plus there’s the [Israeli wildcard,](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/65909) including Tel Aviv’s habit of targeting the infrastructure even of neutral or US-allied actors, and[ its ever-expanding occupation of Syria](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73221)
♦️ The $150-500M in transit fees Syria hopes to get from the pipeline is pocket change next to the $216-$345B the World Bank says it will cost to rebuild the country. Incidentally, before 2011, when jihadists like al-Sharaa flooded in to destroy Syria, its modest oil sector generated ~$3.2B in annual income
♦️ As for Iraq, even if the Syria-bound pipeline was rebuilt and exports via Turkey expanded, it would struggle to meet its pre-Iran war crude exports via Hormuz

A security pact signed in Mecca this week between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey marks one of the clearest indications yet that Gulf states are reconsidering their exclusive reliance on the US.

♦️The threat underscored the White House's willingness to leverage security guarantees as a bargaining chip
Trump's flip-flopping sent a strong signal to Saudi Arabia that the US remains unpredictable regardless of what is agreed or signed, further eroding trust in the partnership
Meanwhile, for China, the Mecca pact represents a significant opportunity to gain access into the Gulf's defense architecture.
🔴China has aggressively marketed its defense systems in the region, leveraging its close military relationship with Pakistan, which depends on Chinese equipment for more than 80% of its arms imports
🔴Pakistan has already deployed JF-17 fighter jets and other Chinese-made systems to Saudi Arabia under bilateral defense agreements, giving them greater visibility and operational experience in the Gulf region
🔴Chinese arms deals typically involve long-term commitments related to maintenance, spare parts, training and logistical support, embedding Chinese systems more deeply into the recipient's military structure
🔴If Saudi Arabia seeks nuclear technology and the US blocks access, China could step in to provide civilian nuclear cooperation, as it has done with Pakistan
🔴China has been steadily expanding its economic footprint in the Gulf through the Belt and Road Initiative and has positioned itself as a reliable alternative to Western partners

⚡️🇮🇷From IRGC veteran to security chief: Mohsen Rezaei takes Iran's top security post
Mohsen Rezaei has been appointed as the new secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, the country's top security body. He replaces Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who took over the position in March 2026 after his predecessor Ali Larijani was killed in an Israeli strike.
The Supreme National Security Council plays a critical role in deciding Iranian policy on the US-Iran conflict. It was the body that approved the June ceasefire memorandum that later collapsed over differences on the Strait of Hormuz.
The appointment, made by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and formalised by President Pezeshkian, places the former IRGC commander at the heart of Iran's wartime decision-making.
A career that mirrors the Islamic Republic's journey
🟥Born in 1954 in Khuzestan province, Rezai was arrested by the Shah's SAVAK secret police in 1971 and later helped draft the IRGC's founding charter after the 1979 revolution
🟥At just 27, he was appointed IRGC commander-in-chief by Imam Khomeini – a post he held for 16 years, making him the longest-serving commander in the force's history
🟥His tenure covered the entirety of the Iran-Iraq War, where he commanded major operations
After stepping down in 1997, Rezaei served for 24 years as secretary of the Expediency Discernment Council. He later entered electoral politics, running for president four times between 2005 and 2021. Under President Raisi, he served as vice president for economic affairs. In March 2026, Khamenei appointed him as his military adviser.
What this means for Iranian decision-making?
Analysts say Rezaei's appointment signals the further consolidation of power by Iran's security establishment. Rezaei has been a constant presence at the highest levels of Iranian politics and security for over four decades. His elevation also reflects the growing influence of the IRGC in shaping state policy, following its major role in repelling US attacks.
👉While Rezaei's appointment does not necessarily mean Iran is moving toward a more hard-line stance, it comes amid increasingly assertive Iranian demands in negotiations with Trump administration. 
➡️Iran has insisted on its right to control the Strait of Hormuz and has rejected any deal that does not include a lifting of all sanctions. 
➡️Iran's position has hardened since the collapse of the June ceasefire, with officials stating that future negotiations must be based on mutual respect and non-interference in Iran's internal affairs.
